**GNU counts newlines, not lines.** cat's main loop keeps `newlines`, the
number of newlines in a row it has just seen. Two in a row mean one empty
line. With `-s`, once that count reaches two, further newlines are
dropped. It's the same state machine as yours with a different counter.

**Where -s is useful.** Text generated by templates or `sed` deletions
often leaves holes of several blank lines. `cat -s` tidies them up without
touching anything else. `man` pages go through something similar.

**`continue` vs a flag variable.** `continue` keeps the skipped case to
one line, but it skips *everything* below it in the loop body. If you
later add code at the bottom of the loop that must run for every byte, it
won't. That's worth remembering when a loop grows.
